payload.problem_statement: Designing and explaining where a lunar mass-driver projectile will land is currently either trivial-but-wrong or correct-but-inaccessible. Free online projectile calculators assume a flat Earth, Earth gravity (~9.81 m/s^2), and often drag — none of which apply to the Moon (~1.62 m/s^2 gravity, ~1737 km radius, no atmosphere); at mass-driver velocities the Moon's curvature dominates, so flat parabolic formulas are materially wrong. Professional mission-design suites (NASA GMAT, AGI STK) are correct but heavy, desktop-licensed, expensive, and aimed at full orbital missions — overkill for a student, educator, or concept designer who wants a 10-second in-browser what-if. No fast, in-browser, 3D-visualized tool exists for lunar mass-driver ballistics: the niche between toy projectile calculators and full mission-design suites is empty.

assumptions: The Moon is the only gravitating body; the projectile is a point mass with no post-launch thrust, no lift, and no drag (no atmosphere).
Gravity is modeled as central inverse-square (not constant-g) so trajectories stay valid for long hops and near-escape velocities (~2.38 km/s lunar escape).
The mass driver imparts an instantaneous muzzle velocity at a fixed elevation and azimuth at the surface.
The target/delivery point is a static location on the lunar surface.
Computation runs client-side in a modern WebGL-capable browser; no backend is needed for the MVP.
The product is a benign logistics/education tool pending clarification of the delivery-vs-strike ambiguity.
unknowns: Intent: logistics delivery (benign) vs. strike/weaponized — the source phrase 'доставки/поражения' supports both and materially changes scope, ethics, and regulatory posture; unresolved.
Required physics fidelity: flat-surface parabola vs. central-gravity/Keplerian — sets core solver complexity and the toy-vs-tool positioning; unresolved.
Whether lunar rotation (Coriolis) and lunar mass concentrations (mascons, which measurably destabilize low lunar orbits) must be modeled.
Performance target — trajectories per second, max simultaneous projectiles, and minimum supported device class — is unspecified.
No confirmed sponsor/customer artifacts exist; unknown whether there is a real customer or this is a speculative/educational product.
Export-control (ITAR/EAR) treatment of launch/trajectory software and Outer Space Treaty / Artemis Accords implications are unconfirmed and depend on the intent resolution.
risks: Regulatory/ethical (high, conditional): the 'strike point' reading would make this a space-weapons concept, invoking export control and space-weapons norms.

Domain accuracy (high): simplified physics (flat Earth, constant-g) presented as authoritative is misleading; mascons and rotation can materially change real results — assumptions must be labeled and a defensible fidelity level chosen.
Positioning (medium): too simple -> redundant with free online calculators; too complex -> competes with GMAT/STK and loses; the lunar/mass-driver/3D/browser niche must be nailed or adoption is zero.
Technical (medium): numerical stability and correct sphere-surface intersection at near-escape velocities; in-browser 3D plus integrator performance on low-end devices; WebGL portability.
Sponsorship/sustainability (medium): greenfield with no confirmed sponsor or user base — risk of building a product with no real users.
payload.candidate_scope: MVP: a single-page, client-side browser app. The user enters a lunar launch position, muzzle velocity, launch azimuth, and launch elevation; the app (1) numerically propagates the projectile under lunar central gravity with no atmosphere, intersecting the lunar sphere to find the impact point, and (2) renders the arc in 3D on a lunar globe with launch/impact markers and orbit-style camera controls. Outputs panel reports impact coordinates, great-circle range, flight time, apogee altitude, and peak speed. Core modules: a physics solver (RK4 integrator or analytic Keplerian surface-intersection), a 3D renderer (Three.js or Babylon.js), and a UI (input form + outputs panel + play/pause) with an assumptions panel so simplified physics is never shown as authoritative. Out of MVP: multi-body/Earth-Moon transfer, mascons, real terrain DEMs, finite-element launch dynamics, warhead/damage/effects, backend accounts, and saved scenarios.

payload.rationale: The MVP is feasible and low-cost to build (standard browser + Three.js/Babylon.js + a lunar-central-gravity solver; the niche is real and unoccupied), but two material clarifications cannot be assumed away reversibly: (1) intent — delivery vs. strike ('доставки/поражения') reshapes ethics, features, and regulatory exposure; (2) physics fidelity target (parabola vs. Keplerian) and whether rotation/mascons are in scope set core solver complexity. A third open question — whether a real sponsor/user base exists — should be confirmed but is not blocking for an MVP-sized client-side build. Chosen 'clarify' over 'go' because the intent and fidelity answers materially change what should be built, and over 'reject' because the concept is sound and the MVP is deliverable once those two questions are answered.
